extracted.intended_audience: general readers of history / readers of a biographical history of Friedrich II
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from a historical biography (Project Gutenberg) describing the Crown-Prince's schooling, character-formation, and literary tendencies; the text evaluates educational methods, moral formation, and literary qualities. Useful for judgments about 18th-century princely education and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education is not a thing of 'vocables'
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is not, and cannot be, a thing of VOCABLES; it is a thing of earnest facts, of capabilities developed, of habits established, of dispositions well dealt with, of tendencies confirmed and tendencies repressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical training and development of capacities and habits matter more than mere verbal instruction. The aim is to make the human soul a 'Cosmos'—to develop the man into DOING something rather than leaving him a singing or eloquent chaos. Emphasize concrete abilities and habits over rote speech-making or empty words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spartan rigor, discipline, frugality, and veracity as foundational
rubrics_metrics.description: There was an inflexible law of discipline everywhere active in his education; a Spartan rigor, frugality, and veracity were inculcated upon him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such discipline, exemplified by apprenticeship to Friedrich Wilhelm, provides a salutary and potent foundation that can conquer other bad elements of schooling. Strictness in matters of conduct and economy prepares a pupil for practical responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy should be both learned and practised
rubrics_metrics.description: Economy he is to study to the bottom; and not only so, but, in another sense of the word, he is to practise economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studying and practising economy (firstly in the economic sense relevant to the time) is treated as a primary useful foundation that will lead to other noble economies and form an essential part of a ruler's education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious piety cannot be taught by catechism and drill alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Piety to God, the nobleness that inspires a human soul to struggle Heavenward, cannot be 'taught' by the most exquisite catechisms, or the most industrious preachings and drillings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silent continual example (of parents or moral exemplars) and a kind of miracle ('the grace of God') are the chief means by which genuine piety is transmitted. Overreliance on abstract catechisms risks producing doubt, hypocrisy, or a 'scraggy' moral existence in the pupil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teachers should open the pupil's mind and give Nature fair-play
rubrics_metrics.description: Duhan, diligent to open his pupil's mind, and give Nature fair-play, had practically found it inexpedient to tie him too rigorously to the arbitrary formal departments where no natural curiosity, but only order from without, urges the ingenious pupil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, encourage instruction in subjects with geniality or practical attractiveness to sustain natural curiosity. Excessive formalism in subjects that do not engage the pupil will lead to superficial compliance rather than deep learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict, arbitrary rules produce only surface obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of such exceeding preciseness, if grounded here and there only on the SIC-VOLO, how could they be always kept, except on the surface and to the eye merely?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overly precise or arbitrary regulations yield compliance that is only superficial. Such formal strictness may be observed outwardly while true understanding or internalization is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secret/forbidden learning can foster clandestine disobedience and alienation
rubrics_metrics.description: The worst fruit of these contraband operations was, that they involved the Boy in clandestine practices, secret disobediences, apt to be found out from time to time, and tended to alienate his Father from him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbidding desirable intellectual pursuits can provoke secret learning and breach of trust; this may produce personal estrangement and other negative social consequences within a household or institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary/ intellectual value: preference for realism and facts over romanticism
rubrics_metrics.description: All his curiosities gravitate towards what exists, what has being and reality round him... Fiction itself is either an expository illustrative garment of Fact, or else is of no value to him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realism and attachment to fact are presented as advantages; Romantic or highly fanciful literature disappoints him. For practical men, literature should illuminate or explain real facts rather than indulge in dreamlike clouds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style qualities: rapidity, vivacity, clarity matter more than perfect orthography
rubrics_metrics.description: His style of French... has real merit. Rapidity, easy vivacity, perfect clearness, here and there a certain quaint expressiveness... His spelling ... is very bad. And as for punctuation, he never could understand the mystery of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear, lively, and expressive communication is of high value even if spelling and punctuation are imperfect; such superficial defects may be tolerated when the essentials of sense and articulation are good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should shape character: develop dispositions and repress tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a thing of capabilities developed, of habits established, of dispositions well dealt with, of tendencies confirmed and tendencies repressed:--a laborious separating of the character into two FIRMAMENTS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond imparting knowledge, schooling must laboriously form the character—confirm desirable tendencies and repress harmful ones—so that the person's inner dispositions align with effective action and moral duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardship and early adversity can produce endurance and useful self-command
rubrics_metrics.description: Out of which there might have come incalculable damage to the young man, had his natural assimilative powers... been less considerable. As it was, he gained self-help from it; gained reticence, the power to keep his own counsel; and did not let the hypocrisy take hold of him, or be other than a hateful compulsory masquerade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Difficult schooling and stern parental demands can cultivate endurance, self-discipline, and reserve—traits valuable for public life—if the pupil has sufficient inner resources to assimilate the lessons productively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste for facts and history is an important intellectual virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: We notice with pleasure a lively taste for facts in the little Boy; which continued to be the taste of the Man... He read History, where he could find it readable, to the end of his life; and had early begun reading it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encouraging a durable interest in factual knowledge, especially history, cultivates a practical intellect and is an asset for future statesmanship and informed action.
